html:
The voyage of the sailing ship Dunedin from Port Chalmers in New Zealand to London in 1882, carrying the first full cargo of frozen meat to cross the world successfully. It founded New Zealand's meat export trade.

New Zealand had millions of sheep but could sell only their wool, tallow and skins; the meat was far too far from any big market. The ship was fitted with a coal fired refrigeration machine that froze the meat and kept it frozen through the tropics. It carried about 5,000 sheep carcasses. The voyage took some three months, and the meat sold well in London.

Within a few years freezing works were built across New Zealand and refrigerated steamships carried lamb, mutton, butter and cheese to Britain. Farming shifted toward meat and dairy, and New Zealand became, in effect, a farm for Britain until Britain joined the European Economic Community in 1973. The same technology helped Argentina and Australia export meat. The Dunedin herself vanished at sea in 1890. See also merino sheep.
